title: Kerala Reports 105 Chikungunya Cases as Monsoon Fuels Outbreak Fears
excerpt: Health authorities have intensified mosquito control across four districts as confirmed cases rise during peak monsoon season — a warning for NRIs planning trips to Kerala.
body:
• Kerala has reported 105 confirmed chikungunya cases across four districts: Thiruvananthapuram, Alappuzha, Ernakulam, and Kozhikode
  • The outbreak coincides with peak monsoon season, which creates ideal mosquito breeding conditions
  • Health authorities have deployed entomologists, epidemiologists, and medical specialists; each affected district received ₹5 lakh for prevention efforts
  • Two FDA-approved chikungunya vaccines exist for adults — travelers to Kerala should consult their doctors before visiting

Kerala's Health Department has confirmed 105 cases of chikungunya fever across four districts, prompting intensified prevention measures as the state's monsoon season creates optimal conditions for the Aedes mosquitoes that transmit the virus.

Four Districts Affected

The confirmed cases span Thiruvananthapuram, Alappuzha, Ernakulam, and Kozhikode — districts that together cover much of Kerala's coastline and are popular destinations for NRI visitors during the monsoon and Onam festival season. NDTV reported the case count at 105, while News18 highlighted concerns about symptoms in children that parents should watch for.

Kerala Health Minister Sreemathy addressed allegations of a delayed response, clarifying that deaths reported in the Cherthala taluk of Alappuzha district were caused by leptospirosis and underlying conditions such as heart disease, not chikungunya. "Most of those who died were suffering from chronic diseases, which were further complicated by the onset of viral fever," the minister said, according to Medindia.

What Travelers Need to Know

"Medicine stocks have been replenished at healthcare facilities across the affected areas, and mosquito control campaigns are "in full swing," according to state health officials."

Chikungunya symptoms typically appear four to eight days after a mosquito bite and include sudden high fever, severe joint pain — particularly in the hands, wrists, ankles, and knees — muscle pain, headache, fatigue, nausea, and rash. The joint pain can be debilitating and may persist for weeks, months, or in some cases years, according to the World Health Organization.

The disease is transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes — the same species that spread dengue and Zika. These mosquitoes are most active during early morning and late afternoon hours, making daytime outdoor activities the highest-risk period.

"Travelers at increased risk for more severe disease, including travelers with underlying medical conditions and women late in their pregnancy, might consider avoiding travel to areas with ongoing chikungunya outbreaks."

— CDC Yellow Book, travel health advisory

Most patients recover fully, but complications — including eye, heart, and neurological problems — can occur, particularly in newborns, elderly individuals, and people with conditions like diabetes or hypertension. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management relies on rest, fluids, and pain relief with acetaminophen. The CDC recommends against using NSAIDs until dengue has been ruled out, due to hemorrhage risk.

Prevention Measures in Kerala

The state health department has allocated ₹5 lakh to each affected district and deployed entomologists, epidemiologists, and medical specialists to investigate the outbreak. Vector control programs including fogging operations are underway, with teams working to identify and eliminate mosquito breeding sites.

Medicine stocks have been replenished at healthcare facilities across the affected areas, and mosquito control campaigns are "in full swing," according to state health officials.

Advisory for NRIs Visiting Kerala

With the Onam festival approaching in late August and monsoon tourism drawing visitors to Kerala's backwaters and hill stations, the outbreak timing is particularly relevant for diaspora travelers. The CDC and WHO recommend the following precautions for anyone visiting affected areas:

Use EPA-registered mosquito repellents on exposed skin, particularly those containing DEET, picaridin, or IR3535. Wear long-sleeved clothing and full-length pants, especially during early morning and late afternoon. Sleep in air-conditioned rooms or under insecticide-treated mosquito nets. Avoid areas with standing water — puddles, uncovered containers, drainage ditches — where mosquitoes breed.

Two chikungunya vaccines have received FDA approval for adults: IXCHIQ (a live-attenuated vaccine) and Vimkunya (a virus-like particle vaccine), both showing approximately 98-99% seroprotection rates. However, IXCHIQ has been paused for use in persons over 60 due to safety concerns. Both vaccines are currently recommended by the CDC specifically for travelers visiting areas with declared outbreaks.

NRIs planning trips to Kerala should consult their healthcare providers about vaccination and take preventive measures seriously, particularly those traveling with young children, pregnant women, or elderly family members.
